CausalChain: Phytochemical exposure (e.g., resveratrol/curcumin) -> selective binding to lncRNA structural motifs (e.g., MALAT1 triple helix) -> conformational change in lncRNA -> disrupted interaction with chromatin modifiers/RNA-binding proteins -> downregulation of oncogenic gene programs -> compensatory upregulation/alteration of mitochondrial lncRNAs -> activation of mitochondrial apoptotic and metabolic reprogramming pathways -> increased tumor cell chemosensitivity
Hypothesis: Phytochemical-derived small molecules can remodel the structure of oncogenic lncRNAs in the nucleus, thereby disrupting pro-tumorigenic gene regulation while simultaneously triggering mitochondrial lncRNA‐mediated apoptotic signaling. This dual mechanism may reprogram tumor metabolism and enhance the efficacy of conventional chemotherapies.
Abstract: Recent insights into long non‐coding RNA (lncRNA) biology have revealed their dual roles in nuclear gene regulation and mitochondrial signaling, implicating them as crucial modulators in disease progression and treatment response. Building on observations that phytochemicals such as resveratrol and curcumin can modulate lncRNA activity, we propose a novel model in which specific natural compound–derived small molecules bind to conserved structural elements (e.g., the MALAT1 triple helix) to alter lncRNA conformation and associated protein interactions. This binding not only disrupts oncogenic chromatin remodeling but also triggers compensatory changes in mitochondrial lncRNA processing that activate apoptosis-related pathways. Such a dual-action axis may facilitate metabolic reprogramming in tumor cells and sensitize them to chemotherapeutic agents. Here, we describe the underlying molecular cascade and outline potential therapeutic strategies targeting this inter-organelle lncRNA network.
